contents.text: Use the passage about cash to answer the question below.

pieces.text: is money in the form of metal coins or paper bills. Cash has many advantages. It is quick and easy to use for small purchases. There are no extra fees or interest charges for using cash. Since cash is money that you physically hold and pay with, it is difficult to spend more money than you have. You don't need to have a bank account to use cash, either. Also, most businesses accept cash for in-person payments, even if they do not accept other forms of payment.

textContent.text: Cash also has several disadvantages. There is no easy way to prove ownership of cash. So, it is difficult to recover cash if it is lost, stolen, or destroyed. Cash also does not provide a record of your purchase if you lose your receipt. Additionally, online purchases cannot be made with cash. And many companies will not accept cash sent by mail.

contents.text: Use the passage about checks to answer the question below.

pieces.text: A

is a piece of paper that lets you pay for something using the money in your bank account. With a check, you write down how much money you want to pay and who you are paying the money to. The other person takes the check to the bank to get the money.

textContent.text: Checks have many advantages. They give you access to all of the money in your bank account, without having to carry the cash with you. Checks can be canceled if they are lost or stolen, so they are safer to carry and send in the mail than cash. As long as you have enough money in your bank account, there are no extra fees for using checks. Checks also give you a record of your purchases to help keep track of your spending.

Checks also have several disadvantages. Writing a check takes longer than paying with cash. To have a checkbook, you need to open a checking account at a bank. If you write a check for more money than you have in your account, you will likely be charged fees by your bank and by the business that received your check. Some businesses will not accept checks, especially for online purchases. And criminals can steal checks and cash them, if you don't cancel missing checks right away.

pieces.text: A

is a piece of paper that lets you pay for something using the money in your bank account. With a check, you write down how much money you want to pay and who you are paying the money to. The other person takes the check to the bank to get the money.

textContent.text: Checks have many advantages. They give you access to all of the money in your bank account, without having to carry the cash with you. Checks can be canceled if they are lost or stolen, so they are safer to carry and send in the mail than cash. As long as you have enough money in your bank account, there are no extra fees for using checks. Checks also give you a record of your purchases to help keep track of your spending.

Checks also have several disadvantages. Writing a check takes longer than paying with cash. To have a checkbook, you need to open a checking account at a bank. If you write a check for more money than you have in your account, you will likely be charged fees by your bank and by the business that received your check. Some businesses will not accept checks, especially for online purchases. And criminals can steal checks and cash them, if you don't cancel missing checks right away.

pieces.text: A

is a piece of paper that lets you pay for something using the money in your bank account. With a check, you write down how much money you want to pay and who you are paying the money to. The other person takes the check to the bank to get the money.

textContent.text: Checks have many advantages. They give you access to all of the money in your bank account, without having to carry the cash with you. Checks can be canceled if they are lost or stolen, so they are safer to carry and send in the mail than cash. As long as you have enough money in your bank account, there are no extra fees for using checks. Checks also give you a record of your purchases to help keep track of your spending.

Checks also have several disadvantages. Writing a check takes longer than paying with cash. To have a checkbook, you need to open a checking account at a bank. If you write a check for more money than you have in your account, you will likely be charged fees by your bank and by the business that received your check. Some businesses will not accept checks, especially for online purchases. And criminals can steal checks and cash them, if you don't cancel missing checks right away.

textContent.text: People existed in lower, chaotic worlds before coming to this world. In each of the lower worlds, people fought and behaved badly, and they fled to higher worlds. contents.text: Read about villages of the Great Plains. Then answer the question below.

title.text: Mandan and Hidatsa earthen dwellings, On-A-Slant Indian Village

textContent.text: Villages across the Great Plains region had many similarities, whether their people were sedentary or semi-sedentary.

Most villages were near rivers or streams so people could access fresh water. Villages had nearby fields where people grew beans, corn, and squash. Sunflowers were another common crop. People ate sunflower seeds, ground them into flour, and used sunflower oil to cook.

Most villages had permanent dwellings known as earth lodges. Earth lodges could house between thirty and fifty people. Villages ranged in size from a few hundred to a few thousand people. The image shows a re-creation of a Mandan village in North Dakota. The original village had about 75 earth lodges at its largest, with about 1,000 people living there.

Living near rivers allowed people to grow crops like corn and sunflowers.

contents.text: Of all the animals people hunted in the Great Plains, bison were by far the most important. For thousands of years, Native people hunted bison on foot. Once horses became part of Great Plains culture, people hunted on horseback.
Look at the diagram showing several traditional uses of bison parts. Then answer the question below.

alternativeText.text: A diagram showing how Native American people used different parts of the bison. Native people used hide to make moccasins, clothing, tipi covers, bedding drums, saddles, and headdresses. People used bison hair to make paintbrushes, rope, and pillows. Horns were used as spoons, cups, and toys. People ate bison meat, including the tongue. They used the sinew to make bow strings. They used bison fat for cooking oil and to make soap. People made needles, knives, arrowheads, and various tools from bison bone. They used bison stomachs to make cups, pots, dishes, and buckets. Bison hooves were used for rattles and to make glue.

Horns were used as spoons, cups, and toys. People ate bison meat, including the tongue. They used the sinew to make bow strings. They used bison fat for cooking oil and to make soap. People made needles, knives, arrowheads, and various tools from bison bone. They used bison stomachs to make cups, pots, dishes, and buckets. Bison hooves were used for rattles and to make glue.

contents.text: Read about villages of the Great Plains. Then answer the question below.

title.text: Mandan and Hidatsa earthen dwellings, On-A-Slant Indian Village

textContent.text: Villages across the Great Plains region had many similarities, whether their people were sedentary or semi-sedentary.

Most villages were near rivers or streams so people could access fresh water. Villages had nearby fields where people grew beans, corn, and squash. Sunflowers were another common crop. People ate sunflower seeds, ground them into flour, and used sunflower oil to cook.

Most villages had permanent dwellings known as earth lodges. Earth lodges could house between thirty and fifty people. Villages ranged in size from a few hundred to a few thousand people. The image shows a re-creation of a Mandan village in North Dakota. The original village had about 75 earth lodges at its largest, with about 1,000 people living there.

People in Great Plains villages built earth lodges near fresh water.

contents.text: Great Plains peoples used both permanent and portable shelters. Read the passages about shelters. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: were portable, cone-shaped houses made of wooden frames covered in bison hide. Tipis varied in size but often held up to ten people. Openings at the top of the structure allowed smoke from small cooking fires to escape. Tipis could be set up and taken down fairly quickly. Their portability made tipis ideal structures for people who traveled frequently, like the nomadic Siksikaitsitapi people.

were permanent dwellings supported by wooden posts. The lodges were large enough to house multiple families, often between thirty and fifty people. Inside, earth lodges had underground pits for storing food and central hearths for building fires. Many people across the region, from the Mandan in present-day North Dakota to the Pawnee in present-day Nebraska and Kansas, built earth lodges.

contents.text: Of all the animals people hunted in the Great Plains, bison were by far the most important. For thousands of years, Native people hunted bison on foot. Once horses became part of Great Plains culture, people hunted on horseback.
Look at the diagram showing several traditional uses of bison parts. Then answer the question below.

alternativeText.text: A diagram showing how Native American people used different parts of the bison. Native people used hide to make moccasins, clothing, tipi covers, bedding drums, saddles, and headdresses. People used bison hair to make paintbrushes, rope, and pillows. Horns were used as spoons, cups, and toys. People ate bison meat, including the tongue. They used the sinew to make bow strings. They used bison fat for cooking oil and to make soap. People made needles, knives, arrowheads, and various tools from bison bone. They used bison stomachs to make cups, pots, dishes, and buckets. Bison hooves were used for rattles and to make glue.

contents.text: Of all the animals people hunted in the Great Plains, bison were by far the most important. For thousands of years, Native people hunted bison on foot. Once horses became part of Great Plains culture, people hunted on horseback.
Look at the diagram showing several traditional uses of bison parts. Then answer the question below.

alternativeText.text: A diagram showing how Native American people used different parts of the bison. Native people used hide to make moccasins, clothing, tipi covers, bedding drums, saddles, and headdresses. People used bison hair to make paintbrushes, rope, and pillows. Horns were used as spoons, cups, and toys. People ate bison meat, including the tongue. They used the sinew to make bow strings. They used bison fat for cooking oil and to make soap. People made needles, knives, arrowheads, and various tools from bison bone. They used bison stomachs to make cups, pots, dishes, and buckets. Bison hooves were used for rattles and to make glue.

contents.text: Since people in the Great Plains had such different lifestyles, they each had unique goods to offer other communities. Read the information. Then answer the question below.

elements.text: Nomadic people valued and ate corn, even though they did not farm it.
Sedentary communities mainly farmed, as opposed to hunting. However, they used tools made from bison parts, like garden hoes made from bison shoulder blades.
Groups living in the southern plains had cotton fabric and turquoise from the Southwest region hundreds of miles away.
People in the northern plains had items made from coastal Atlantic shells, even though no part of the Great Plains borders the Atlantic Ocean.

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans mysteriously abandoned their largest settlements in the 1200s. Read the passage about what archaeologists think may have happened to the Ancestral Pueblo. Then follow the directions below.

textContent.text: Archaeologists don't know for sure why the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements. Some archaeologists think they left because of environmental issues. By examining the sizes of tree rings, archaeologists discovered that there was a drought when these sites were abandoned. Pollen remains from flowers show that winters were becoming colder and drier, which could make farming more difficult. Archaeologists also think that people cut down trees faster than they could be regrown. This deforestation may have caused a shortage of resources.

Other archaeologists think that the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements because of social issues. Archaeologists have found unburied skeletons with crushed skulls, which suggests there may have been a war. They have also found that people started building more settlements with high walls. These walls were likely meant to protect against enemy attacks. Archaeologists have also found religious artwork suggesting the development of a new religion that may have drawn Ancestral Puebloans away from their settlements.

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans mysteriously abandoned their largest settlements in the 1200s. Read the passage about what archaeologists think may have happened to the Ancestral Pueblo. Then follow the directions below.

textContent.text: Archaeologists don't know for sure why the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements. Some archaeologists think they left because of environmental issues. By examining the sizes of tree rings, archaeologists discovered that there was a drought when these sites were abandoned. Pollen remains from flowers show that winters were becoming colder and drier, which could make farming more difficult. Archaeologists also think that people cut down trees faster than they could be regrown. This deforestation may have caused a shortage of resources.

Other archaeologists think that the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements because of social issues. Archaeologists have found unburied skeletons with crushed skulls, which suggests there may have been a war. They have also found that people started building more settlements with high walls. These walls were likely meant to protect against enemy attacks. Archaeologists have also found religious artwork suggesting the development of a new religion that may have drawn Ancestral Puebloans away from their settlements.

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans mysteriously abandoned their largest settlements in the 1200s. Read the passage about what archaeologists think may have happened to the Ancestral Pueblo. Then follow the directions below.

textContent.text: Archaeologists don't know for sure why the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements. Some archaeologists think they left because of environmental issues. By examining the sizes of tree rings, archaeologists discovered that there was a drought when these sites were abandoned. Pollen remains from flowers show that winters were becoming colder and drier, which could make farming more difficult. Archaeologists also think that people cut down trees faster than they could be regrown. This deforestation may have caused a shortage of resources.

Other archaeologists think that the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements because of social issues. Archaeologists have found unburied skeletons with crushed skulls, which suggests there may have been a war. They have also found that people started building more settlements with high walls. These walls were likely meant to protect against enemy attacks. Archaeologists have also found religious artwork suggesting the development of a new religion that may have drawn Ancestral Puebloans away from their settlements.

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans mysteriously abandoned their largest settlements in the 1200s. Read the passage about what archaeologists think may have happened to the Ancestral Pueblo. Then follow the directions below.

textContent.text: Archaeologists don't know for sure why the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements. Some archaeologists think they left because of environmental issues. By examining the sizes of tree rings, archaeologists discovered that there was a drought when these sites were abandoned. Pollen remains from flowers show that winters were becoming colder and drier, which could make farming more difficult. Archaeologists also think that people cut down trees faster than they could be regrown. This deforestation may have caused a shortage of resources.

Other archaeologists think that the Ancestral Puebloans left their settlements because of social issues. Archaeologists have found unburied skeletons with crushed skulls, which suggests there may have been a war. They have also found that people started building more settlements with high walls. These walls were likely meant to protect against enemy attacks. Archaeologists have also found religious artwork suggesting the development of a new religion that may have drawn Ancestral Puebloans away from their settlements.

. As they moved around, bands often interacted with each other, especially to trade. Read the passage about trade in the Great Basin. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: People living in the Great Basin traded weapons used for hunting, dried meat that could be stored for the winter, and tanned animal hides used for clothing and shelter. They often traded with other groups in the Great Basin, but some bands traded with people from other regions, such as the Puebloans in the Southwest. People in the Great Basin used Puebloan pottery to store water and food.

Horses were introduced to the Great Basin in the 1600s. Groups that adopted horses early, such as the Ute, were able to travel quickly across large distances. This helped them hunt larger game and increased their trading opportunities.

contents.text: Some of the most important events celebrated each year were ceremonies. Read about two Great Basin ceremonies. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: People in the Great Basin sometimes went on

, during which they would go into the wilderness alone, often staying several days without food or water. They hoped to have a dream about a spirit animal that could give them powers, such as the ability to run quickly or to heal others. Many people went on their first vision quest when they became a young adult, but they could go on more than one in their lifetime.
The Ute performed the

to ask the Spirit of the Bear for permission to gather food from mountain areas. Each spring, a band or group of bands would kill a bear. Then they would eat its meat during a community feast where people considered the bear's spirit to be an honored guest. For some bands of Ute, this would be the only bear they killed throughout the year. After the feast, they held a dance. The Bear Dance ceremony lasted five days.

pieces.text: Most people in the Great Basin traveled in small family units called
. As they moved around, bands often interacted with each other, especially to trade. Read the passage about trade in the Great Basin. Then follow the directions below.

textContent.text: People living in the Great Basin traded weapons used for hunting, dried meat that could be stored for the winter, and tanned animal hides used for clothing and shelter. They often traded with other groups in the Great Basin, but some bands traded with people from other regions, such as the Puebloans in the Southwest. People in the Great Basin used Puebloan pottery to store water and food.

Horses were introduced to the Great Basin in the 1600s. Groups that adopted horses early, such as the Ute, were able to travel quickly across large distances. This helped them hunt larger game and increased their trading opportunities.

. As they moved around, bands often interacted with each other, especially to trade. Read the passage about trade in the Great Basin. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: People living in the Great Basin traded weapons used for hunting, dried meat that could be stored for the winter, and tanned animal hides used for clothing and shelter. They often traded with other groups in the Great Basin, but some bands traded with people from other regions, such as the Puebloans in the Southwest. People in the Great Basin used Puebloan pottery to store water and food.

Horses were introduced to the Great Basin in the 1600s. Groups that adopted horses early, such as the Ute, were able to travel quickly across large distances. This helped them hunt larger game and increased their trading opportunities.

contents.text: Some of the most important events celebrated each year were ceremonies. Read about two Great Basin ceremonies. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: People in the Great Basin sometimes went on

, during which they would go into the wilderness alone, often staying several days without food or water. They hoped to have a dream about a spirit animal that could give them powers, such as the ability to run quickly or to heal others. Many people went on their first vision quest when they became a young adult, but they could go on more than one in their lifetime.
The Ute performed the

to ask the Spirit of the Bear for permission to gather food from mountain areas. Each spring, a band or group of bands would kill a bear. Then they would eat its meat during a community feast where people considered the bear's spirit to be an honored guest. For some bands of Ute, this would be the only bear they killed throughout the year. After the feast, they held a dance. The Bear Dance ceremony lasted five days.

contents.text: Because Native Pacific Northwest people lived so close to rivers and the ocean, they ate a fish-based diet. Read the passage about salmon and Pacific Northwest Native societies. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Of all the foods Pacific Northwest people ate, salmon was one of the most important. People used special nets to fish for salmon. These small nets were designed to catch salmon while allowing other fish to pass. People also carved canoes with flat bottoms, which made river travel easier. They used poles to steer the canoes upriver to salmon habitats.

pieces.text: Each spring, communities held

at the start of the salmon fishing season. First, each chief chose a fisherman to catch the season's first salmon. The fisherman brought it back to the village, where the women prepared it with honor. Then, another fisherman returned the salmon's bones to the river. After honoring the first salmon, the people feasted. They ate salmon, gave thanks, said prayers, and performed songs and dances. The First Salmon ceremony was one of the most important events of the year.

contents.text: Pacific Northwest people lived in different settlements depending on the season. Read the passage about the different types of settlements they built. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: During mild springs and summers, when food resources were most abundant, Pacific Northwest people migrated to fish, hunt, and gather food. They needed shelters that were transportable and easy to set up in places where food could be acquired. So, Native people built small, portable, lightweight shelters from bark or from grass-like plants called

textContent.text: During winter, Native people needed access to water and protection from the cold. So, they built cedar-plank houses in permanent villages near rivers or streams. These houses could be up to 20 feet wide and 100 feet long, large enough to fit as many as 100 people! Inside, there was usually a shallow firepit in the center of the house, with living space around it. Bunks and shelves ran along the walls. Winter was not a good time to hunt, fish, or gather, so these homes had plenty of space to store preserved foods to eat throughout the winter.

contents.text: Pacific Northwest people lived in different settlements depending on the season. Read the passage about the different types of settlements they built. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: During mild springs and summers, when food resources were most abundant, Pacific Northwest people migrated to fish, hunt, and gather food. They needed shelters that were transportable and easy to set up in places where food could be acquired. So, Native people built small, portable, lightweight shelters from bark or from grass-like plants called

textContent.text: During winter, Native people needed access to water and protection from the cold. So, they built cedar-plank houses in permanent villages near rivers or streams. These houses could be up to 20 feet wide and 100 feet long, large enough to fit as many as 100 people! Inside, there was usually a shallow firepit in the center of the house, with living space around it. Bunks and shelves ran along the walls. Winter was not a good time to hunt, fish, or gather, so these homes had plenty of space to store preserved foods to eat throughout the winter.

contents.text: Because Native Pacific Northwest people lived so close to rivers and the ocean, they ate a fish-based diet. Read the passage about salmon and Pacific Northwest Native societies. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Of all the foods Pacific Northwest people ate, salmon was one of the most important. People used special nets to fish for salmon. These small nets were designed to catch salmon while allowing other fish to pass. People also carved canoes with flat bottoms, which made river travel easier. They used poles to steer the canoes upriver to salmon habitats.

pieces.text: Each spring, communities held

at the start of the salmon fishing season. First, each chief chose a fisherman to catch the season's first salmon. The fisherman brought it back to the village, where the women prepared it with honor. Then, another fisherman returned the salmon's bones to the river. After honoring the first salmon, the people feasted. They ate salmon, gave thanks, said prayers, and performed songs and dances. The First Salmon ceremony was one of the most important events of the year.

contents.text: Because Native Pacific Northwest people lived so close to rivers and the ocean, they ate a fish-based diet. Read the passage about salmon and Pacific Northwest Native societies. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Of all the foods Pacific Northwest people ate, salmon was one of the most important. People used special nets to fish for salmon. These small nets were designed to catch salmon while allowing other fish to pass. People also carved canoes with flat bottoms, which made river travel easier. They used poles to steer the canoes upriver to salmon habitats.

pieces.text: Each spring, communities held

at the start of the salmon fishing season. First, each chief chose a fisherman to catch the season's first salmon. The fisherman brought it back to the village, where the women prepared it with honor. Then, another fisherman returned the salmon's bones to the river. After honoring the first salmon, the people feasted. They ate salmon, gave thanks, said prayers, and performed songs and dances. The First Salmon ceremony was one of the most important events of the year.

contents.text: Pacific Northwest people lived in different settlements depending on the season. Read the passage about the different types of settlements they built. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: During mild springs and summers, when food resources were most abundant, Pacific Northwest people migrated to fish, hunt, and gather food. They needed shelters that were transportable and easy to set up in places where food could be acquired. So, Native people built small, portable, lightweight shelters from bark or from grass-like plants called

textContent.text: During winter, Native people needed access to water and protection from the cold. So, they built cedar-plank houses in permanent villages near rivers or streams. These houses could be up to 20 feet wide and 100 feet long, large enough to fit as many as 100 people! Inside, there was usually a shallow firepit in the center of the house, with living space around it. Bunks and shelves ran along the walls. Winter was not a good time to hunt, fish, or gather, so these homes had plenty of space to store preserved foods to eat throughout the winter.

contents.text: Because Native Pacific Northwest people lived so close to rivers and the ocean, they ate a fish-based diet. Read the passage about salmon and Pacific Northwest Native societies. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Of all the foods Pacific Northwest people ate, salmon was one of the most important. People used special nets to fish for salmon. These small nets were designed to catch salmon while allowing other fish to pass. People also carved canoes with flat bottoms, which made river travel easier. They used poles to steer the canoes upriver to salmon habitats.

pieces.text: Each spring, communities held

at the start of the salmon fishing season. First, each chief chose a fisherman to catch the season's first salmon. The fisherman brought it back to the village, where the women prepared it with honor. Then, another fisherman returned the salmon's bones to the river. After honoring the first salmon, the people feasted. They ate salmon, gave thanks, said prayers, and performed songs and dances. The First Salmon ceremony was one of the most important events of the year.

contents.text: Pacific Northwest people lived in different settlements depending on the season. Read the passage about the different types of settlements they built. Then follow the directions below.

pieces.text: During mild springs and summers, when food resources were most abundant, Pacific Northwest people migrated to fish, hunt, and gather food. They needed shelters that were transportable and easy to set up in places where food could be acquired. So, Native people built small, portable, lightweight shelters from bark or from grass-like plants called

textContent.text: During winter, Native people needed access to water and protection from the cold. So, they built cedar-plank houses in permanent villages near rivers or streams. These houses could be up to 20 feet wide and 100 feet long, large enough to fit as many as 100 people! Inside, there was usually a shallow firepit in the center of the house, with living space around it. Bunks and shelves ran along the walls. Winter was not a good time to hunt, fish, or gather, so these homes had plenty of space to store preserved foods to eat throughout the winter.

contents.text: Native groups in California crafted many boats. People used different materials based on available resources and the boat's intended use. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the northern forests, people made dugout canoes from enormous redwood trees. Craftsmen cut redwood trunks in half, then gently burned and carved away the interior wood. These canoes were strong enough for traveling and fishing in rivers and along the coast.

In the south, the Chumash and Tongva peoples made plank canoes from redwood logs. Craftsmen sawed the logs into planks, then bound them together with a tar-like substance and strong string. People used these canoes for ocean fishing and trading up and down the coast.

content.text: Enormous redwood trees in a forest

mainText.text: Throughout California, Native people used tule (pronounced TOO-lee) reed boats. Tule reeds grow on the banks of relatively calm waters. People dried these flexible reeds, then tightly bound them together to form lightweight boats. They used tule boats to fish, trade, and travel across bays and lakes. Some groups used both tule boats and canoes made from redwood trees, depending on the voyage.

contents.text: Much of California's climate was arid, with most areas not getting enough rainfall for farming to be worth the effort. Instead, Native people gathered food from California's abundant wild plants and trees. In particular, people gathered acorns. Acorns can be dangerous to eat, since they contain a bitter compound that can be poisonous to humans. Even so, about three-quarters of the Native groups of California found a way to eat them.
Native people had a process for making acorns safe to eat. Place the steps of this process in order.

innerComponent.text: People used acorn flour to make all kinds of foods, including bread and soup.
People harvested acorns in late summer and fall. They dried and roasted the acorns to preserve them and to kill any insects that might be on them.
People treated the inedible flour with hot water to remove the poisonous, bitter compound so the flour was safe to eat.
People shelled the preserved acorns and used stones to grind the kernels into flour. But the flour wasn't safe to eat yet.

contents.text: Native groups in California crafted many boats. People used different materials based on available resources and the boat's intended use. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the northern forests, people made dugout canoes from enormous redwood trees. Craftsmen cut redwood trunks in half, then gently burned and carved away the interior wood. These canoes were strong enough for traveling and fishing in rivers and along the coast.

In the south, the Chumash and Tongva peoples made plank canoes from redwood logs. Craftsmen sawed the logs into planks, then bound them together with a tar-like substance and strong string. People used these canoes for ocean fishing and trading up and down the coast.

Throughout California, Native people used tule (pronounced TOO-lee) reed boats. Tule reeds grow on the banks of relatively calm waters. People dried these flexible reeds, then tightly bound them together to form lightweight boats. They used tule boats to fish, trade, and travel across bays and lakes. Some groups used both tule boats and canoes made from redwood trees, depending on the voyage.

contents.text: Much of California's climate was arid, with most areas not getting enough rainfall for farming to be worth the effort. Instead, Native people gathered food from California's abundant wild plants and trees. In particular, people gathered acorns. Acorns can be dangerous to eat, since they contain a bitter compound that can be poisonous to humans. Even so, about three-quarters of the Native groups of California found a way to eat them.
Native people had a process for making acorns safe to eat. Place the steps of this process in order.

innerComponent.text: People used acorn flour to make all kinds of foods, including bread and soup.
People treated the inedible flour with hot water to remove the poisonous, bitter compound so the flour was safe to eat.
People shelled the preserved acorns and used stones to grind the kernels into flour. But the flour wasn't safe to eat yet.
People harvested acorns in late summer and fall. They dried and roasted the acorns to preserve them and to kill any insects that might be on them.

contents.text: Native groups in California crafted many boats. People used different materials based on available resources and the boat's intended use. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the northern forests, people made dugout canoes from enormous redwood trees. Craftsmen cut redwood trunks in half, then gently burned and carved away the interior wood. These canoes were strong enough for traveling and fishing in rivers and along the coast.

In the south, the Chumash and Tongva peoples made plank canoes from redwood logs. Craftsmen sawed the logs into planks, then bound them together with a tar-like substance and strong string. People used these canoes for ocean fishing and trading up and down the coast.

Throughout California, Native people used tule (pronounced TOO-lee) reed boats. Tule reeds grow on the banks of relatively calm waters. People dried these flexible reeds, then tightly bound them together to form lightweight boats. They used tule boats to fish, trade, and travel across bays and lakes. Some groups used both tule boats and canoes made from redwood trees, depending on the voyage.

contents.text: Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Alaska is cold! In winter, temperatures often drop far below freezing. The cold Alaskan climate led to a barren environment where farming crops was impractical. Many areas had very few resources, so some groups of people had to travel long distances to find food.

Throughout Alaska, people spent the warmer months hunting, gathering, and fishing to build up their food supply. To catch whales, seals, and fish, people traveled along the coasts using boats. Native people also spent lots of time in the summer and fall preserving food for the winter, when it was too cold to hunt. During frigid winter months, people stayed inside making tools and clothing.

contents.text: Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Alaska is cold! In winter, temperatures often drop far below freezing. The cold Alaskan climate led to a barren environment where farming crops was impractical. Many areas had very few resources, so some groups of people had to travel long distances to find food.

Throughout Alaska, people spent the warmer months hunting, gathering, and fishing to build up their food supply. To catch whales, seals, and fish, people traveled along the coasts using boats. Native people also spent lots of time in the summer and fall preserving food for the winter, when it was too cold to hunt. During frigid winter months, people stayed inside making tools and clothing.
